# Introduction

## Introduction to the Study

During a typhoon, the Philippines' Twitter/X traffic functions as a real-time distress signal: requests for rescue, reports of flooding and damage, and location clues arrive at a volume that manual review cannot keep pace with, and much of what matters is written in Taglish, the Tagalog–English code-switching typical of Philippine social media. Crisis informatics treats this stream as a natural language processing problem — studies of Philippine disaster tweeting document both its volume and its informational value [@david2016tweeting], and annotated crisis corpora have anchored disaster response research since the CrisisNLP collections [@imran2016twitter], a tradition carried forward in current benchmarks such as HumAID [@alam2021humaid]. Automated triage of disaster messages is therefore not aspirational; what remains open is how to build it for the language and the deployment conditions at hand.

Joint triage is harder than scoring any single dimension, because an operationally useful reading of a message answers three questions at once: what and where it names — named entity recognition (NER) over locations and infrastructure; what is needed — intent classification over humanitarian categories; and how fast — urgency assessment. The three tasks arrive on the same messages, in a low-resource code-mixed variety, and under domain shift: each typhoon is a new distribution, so a model trained on past events is deployed against a disaster it has never seen. The study therefore evaluates out-of-domain by construction, holding out entire typhoon events in a leave-one-disaster-out (LODO) design and reporting per-task Macro-F1.

The natural architecture for the joint problem is one multilingual encoder shared by the three tasks, each with its own lightweight head — hard parameter sharing [@caruana1997multitask]. Sharing also fits the deployment constraint: local inference on commodity hardware avoids recurring cloud costs, privacy exposure of citizen messages, and dependence on connectivity during an outage, and one resident model instead of three reduces both memory and the number of encoder passes per request. But sharing couples training: one task's gradient can pull against another's, degrading a task below its single-task performance — negative transfer. Whether that interference is better handled by uniform scalarization (equal 1:1:1 task weighting), by tuned static weights, or by dynamic gradient surgery — PCGrad, which removes the component of a task's gradient that conflicts with another's [@yu2020gradient] — is the open question this study benchmarks, under identical data, schedules, and tuning budgets.

The study makes four contributions: (i) a self-annotated Taglish common-corpus benchmark, in which every tweet carries all three label sets, evaluated under a leave-one-disaster-out protocol; (ii) a pre-registered benchmark of dynamic versus static multitask balancing under domain divergence; (iii) an inference-efficiency profile of the unified model on commodity hardware, with edge deployment as future work; and (iv) a gradient-conflict diagnostic linking optimization dynamics to per-task transfer. Chapter 2 situates these against the crisis-informatics, code-mixing, and multitask-optimization literatures; Chapter 3 specifies the corpus, protocol, and instruments.

## Background of the Study

<!-- Write last, after Chapter 3. Macro to meso to micro funnel, landing on the two gaps and the four questions stated above. -->

## Statement of the Problem

During a typhoon, response coordinators must triage incoming Taglish (Tagalog–English code-mixed) tweets across three questions at once — what and where, through named entity recognition (NER); what is needed, through intent classification; and how fast, through urgency assessment — at a volume and speed that manual review cannot sustain. Yet every new typhoon is a new distribution: a model trained on past events meets out-of-domain language, event-specific vocabulary, and shifting class balances at deployment time. Taglish itself compounds the difficulty, because code-mixing is unevenly served by multilingual encoders and the low-resource setting leaves little supervision to correct it. Serving one model per task multiplies the memory and compute that commodity hardware must hold, while a single shared-encoder model with task-specific heads reduces that footprint but exposes training to task interference, in which one task's gradient degrades another task's performance — negative transfer. Whether that interference is better mitigated by dynamic gradient surgery than by static task weighting under realistic domain shift — measured per task and per language stratum, not in the aggregate alone — is unsettled, and no pre-registered, out-of-disaster benchmark exists to decide it for this setting. This study addresses that problem.

Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following questions:

**RQ1.** How does a hard parameter-sharing multitask learning (MTL) model compare against task-dedicated single-task learning (STL) baselines in out-of-domain disaster generalization, both in aggregate Macro-F1 (the unweighted mean of per-task Macro-F1) and across Taglish code-mixing strata (English-dominant, Mixed, Tagalog-dominant)?

**RQ2.** What operational efficiency gains — single-sample inference latency and peak RAM/VRAM footprint — does the unified multitask architecture yield on the available commodity hardware relative to all-resident sequential execution of the single-task baselines (the primary baseline) and, where it completes without memory contention, concurrent execution, and does it retain practical task performance on every target task?

**RQ3.** To what extent does directional gradient-conflict surgery (PCGrad) mitigate task-level negative transfer, $\mathrm{NT}_t = \mathrm{Macro\text{-}F1}_{\mathrm{STL},t} - \mathrm{Macro\text{-}F1}_{\mathrm{MTL},t}$, relative to uniform scalarization (1:1:1) and an inner-fold tuned static scalarization baseline under leave-one-disaster-out (LODO) domain shift?

**RQ4.** How do inter-task gradient-conflict frequencies — the proportion of batches with $\cos(g_i, g_j) < 0$ on the final shared encoder layer, measured under uniform scalarization — associate with forward changes in checkpoint-matched per-task F1 ($\Delta F1_t(c \to c{+}1)$), and does conflict concentrate between the token-level head (NER) and the sequence-level heads (intent, urgency)?

## Objectives of the Study

The general objective of the study is to benchmark dynamic against static multitask balancing for the joint triage of Taglish disaster tweets on one shared multilingual encoder, under leave-one-disaster-out domain shift, with per-task negative-transfer accounting and an inference-efficiency profile on commodity hardware. Specifically, the study aims:

**RO1.** To benchmark the shared-encoder multitask model against dedicated single-task baselines across $K$ leave-one-disaster-out folds and $S$ seeds, in aggregate Macro-F1 on fold-level paired differences and across code-mixing strata on the pooled out-of-fold construction. *(Baseline Analysis; Empirical Benchmarking.)*

**RO2.** To profile the unified model's single-sample inference latency and peak memory against all-resident sequential execution of the single-task baselines on the designated commodity machine, and to assess per-task performance retention against the frozen margin $\epsilon$. *(Empirical Benchmarking; Comparative Validation.)*

**RO3.** To contrast uniform scalarization, inner-fold tuned static scalarization, and PCGrad under identical training schedules, data, and seeds, and to quantify per-task negative transfer $\mathrm{NT}_t$ with fold-level confidence intervals. *(Design and Artifact Creation; Comparative Validation.)*

**RO4.** To instrument the uniform-scalarization arm with side-effect-free per-task gradient logging, testing whether conflict frequency concentrates between the token-level and sequence-level heads and whether it tracks forward changes in checkpoint-matched per-task F1 ($\Delta F1_t(c \to c{+}1)$). *(Design and Artifact Creation — diagnostic instrumentation; Empirical Benchmarking.)*

## Hypothesis of the Study

Following the pre-registered protocol, the hypotheses are partitioned by evidential role. Four are confirmatory and are stated as formal null/alternative pairs; the remainder are descriptive or non-superiority assessments whose verdicts follow pre-declared decision rules rather than significance tests, and none of the latter is presented as a test. No family-wise control is applied across hypotheses; Holm correction applies only within H1b's two-stratum family. Symbol forms are formalized in Chapter 3.

**H1a (aggregate superiority — confirmatory).** On fold-level paired differences ($N = K$): $H_0{:}\ \mu_{\mathrm{MTL}} - \mu_{\mathrm{STL}} \le 0$ versus $H_1{:}\ \mu_{\mathrm{MTL}} - \mu_{\mathrm{STL}} > 0$, evaluated by an exact paired sign-flip permutation at one-sided $\alpha = .05$. If the test fails to reject, the result is reported with its confidence interval and assessed against the H2b retention bound; "non-inferiority" language is reserved for H2b.

**H1b (stratified low-resource transfer — confirmatory).** Within the Tagalog-dominant and Mixed strata, the pooled out-of-fold transfer delta is positive, verified by one-sided cluster-paired bootstrap CI lower bounds excluding zero, Holm-corrected across the two strata (97.5%/95% bounds). The English-dominant stratum is reported descriptively as a contrast, and stratum × class cells below the pre-registered support threshold ($n < 25$ unique examples) are reported descriptively and excluded from the tested family.

**H3a (aggregate optimization contrast — confirmatory).** PCGrad achieves higher aggregate Macro-F1 than uniform scalarization on fold-level paired differences: $H_0{:}\ \mu_{\mathrm{agg}}(\mathrm{PCGrad}) - \mu_{\mathrm{agg}}(\mathrm{Uniform}) \le 0$ versus $H_1{:}\ > 0$ (exact paired permutation, $N = K$). The hypothesis is stated on the aggregate directly because the fold-level difference in summed negative transfer between two multitask arms is algebraically identical to $T$ times the aggregate Macro-F1 difference, so a $\sum \mathrm{NT}$-framed test would measure the same quantity under a different label; per-task $\mathrm{NT}_t$ differences are reported with fold-level CIs and no per-task confirmatory test.

**H4a (granularity asymmetry — confirmatory).** Conflict frequency between the token-level head and the sequence-level heads exceeds that between the two sequence-level heads, on fold-averaged means: $H_0{:}\ \bar\kappa_{\mathrm{NER,seq}} \le \bar\kappa_{\mathrm{seq,seq}}$ versus $H_1{:}\ \bar\kappa_{\mathrm{NER,seq}} > \bar\kappa_{\mathrm{seq,seq}}$ (exact paired permutation, $N = K$; all three pairwise means are reported alongside the contrast).

**H2a (resource footprint — descriptive, architectural expectation).** Replacing three encoder stacks with one shared encoder reduces the dominant memory and compute component to roughly one-third, so a ≥50% reduction in peak memory and per-sample latency versus all-resident sequential single-task execution is expected; the memory expectation carries over unchanged to concurrent execution (same resident footprint), while no latency ordering versus concurrent execution is claimed; under load/unload swapping the memory claim does not apply. No inferential test.

**H2b (bounded operational degradation — descriptive).** Every task satisfies $\Delta\mathrm{Macro\text{-}F1}_t \ge -\epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is frozen at $1.5\times$ the pooled seed-level SD of single-task Macro-F1, computed from all $K$ single-task folds before any multitask run. Retention holds if and only if all three tasks clear the bound, each with its 95% CI reported alongside the point estimate.

**H3b (static baseline competitiveness — non-superiority assessment).** PCGrad will show no practically meaningful advantage over tuned static scalarization: support requires the 90% two-sided CI of the fold-level paired difference (PCGrad − tuned) in aggregate Macro-F1 to have its upper bound below the frozen margin $\delta_{\mathrm{opt}} = 0.01$; if additionally the lower bound exceeds $-\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}$, the stronger practical-equivalence (TOST-style) conclusion is reported. This expectation follows @xin2022current and @kurin2022defense.

**H4b (diagnostic transfer coupling — descriptive).** High conflict frequency in a checkpoint window is followed by reduced transfer growth: supported if the median of the per-(run, task) lead–lag correlations between task-mean conflict frequency $\kappa_t(c)$ and forward changes $\Delta F1_t(c \to c{+}1)$ is negative, with the full distribution (median and IQR over the $K \times S \times T$ per-(run, task) correlations) and trajectory visualizations reported. A competing hypothesis is pre-registered — gradient conflict and negative transfer are not strongly coupled, and conflict can be benign or act as regularization [@jiang2023forkmerge] — so a near-zero or positive median is an interpretable outcome, not a null failure.

## Theoretical Framework of the Study

The theoretical framework assembles the theories that explain why the relationships under test should hold as designed. Each anchor states the concepts it contributes, the assumption it carries, and the hypothesis family that rests on it; together they predict where multitask sharing should help, where it should hurt, and what any observed difference must exceed before it matters.

**Hard parameter sharing and inductive transfer.** @caruana1997multitask defined multitask learning as inductive transfer: the training signals of related tasks serve as an inductive bias while the tasks are learned in parallel through a shared representation, and hard parameter sharing — one shared encoder carrying task-specific heads — is its standard form in deep learning [@ruder2017overview]. The theory contributes the study's central expectation: tasks related closely enough to share structure improve together, so the unified model can match or exceed dedicated single-task baselines (H1a); and because the same sharing leaves one encoder resident where three models would otherwise sit, it also carries the architectural footprint expectation (H2a). It admits its own failure mode — negative transfer, in which a task is left worse by sharing than by training alone [@ruder2017overview] — which the study measures per task as $\mathrm{NT}_t$ rather than in the aggregate alone. The assumption is task relatedness, and the design builds it in rather than presuming it: the three triage tasks are annotated on the same messages over a common corpus, so inputs are identical across arms and any performance difference is attributable to parameter sharing with cross-task supervision, not to differences in data.

**Multi-task gradient conflict.** @yu2020gradient supply the accepted mechanistic account of that failure mode: when per-task gradients conflict in direction, the shared parameters follow a compromise that can serve neither task, and projecting each conflicting gradient onto the plane orthogonal to the other removes the conflicting component — the PCGrad rule this study instantiates as its dynamic balancing arm. The theory grounds the optimization contrast (H3a) and the diagnostic (H4): if conflict drives interference, then removing it should improve aggregate performance over uniform scalarization, and conflict frequency $\kappa$ — the proportion of batches whose gradient cosine $\cos(g_i, g_j)$ is negative — should concentrate where the architecture mixes granularities, between the token-level named entity recognition head and the sequence-level heads. The assumption is contestable, and the framework carries the rival account explicitly: @jiang2023forkmerge find that gradient conflict is frequent even when transfer is beneficial, that task gradients are often near-orthogonal, and that conflict can act as regularization rather than interference. The study therefore pre-registers both readings — H4a/H4b alongside a competing hypothesis — so that a near-zero coupling between conflict and transfer is an interpretable outcome rather than a failed test.

**Code-switching linguistics and the code-mixing index.** The matrix language frame of Myers-Scotton [-@myersscotton1993duelling] holds that one language supplies the morphosyntactic frame of a code-switched utterance while the other supplies embedded material; the reviewers of that account dispute the frequency criterion that identifies the frame [@muysken1995review], so the study does not rely on it. What survives dispute is that mixing is systematic and therefore measurable: the code-mixing index (CMI) quantifies a message's mixing as the share of its language-dependent tokens outside its matrix language [@gamback2016comparing], and CMI bands partition the corpus into English-dominant, Mixed, and Tagalog-dominant strata. The theory grounds the stratified hypothesis (H1b): if multilingual pretraining serves its languages unevenly, the benefit of sharing should vary across strata, and the low-resource strata are where transfer matters most for deployment. It carries two assumptions the design freezes before annotation — the CMI formulation and the treatment of borrowings and cognates in language identification — because both determine stratum membership and corpus inclusion alike.

**Distribution shift and out-of-domain generalization.** Each typhoon is a new distribution over language use, named entities, event vocabulary, and class balance, so a triage model's deployment condition is out-of-domain by default: it is trained on past events and serves one it has never seen. Leave-one-disaster-out operationalizes that condition directly — every performance estimate is event-level out-of-domain generalization, and no held-out-event data informs model selection. The theory grounds the estimand of RQ1 through RQ3: what the study benchmarks is transfer across disasters, not accuracy within one. It carries the assumption that fold-level estimates speak to future events, which the design bounds by acknowledging the $N = K$ resolution of its fold-level inference rather than correcting it; the within-disaster dev leakage the protocol admits is accepted because the selection policy is identical across arms and therefore protects the comparison. <!-- CITE: dataset-shift theory anchor, not yet registered. Candidates: Ben-David et al. (2010), "A theory of learning from different domains," Machine Learning 79, 151–175; Moreno-Torres et al. (2012), "A unifying view on dataset shift in classification," Pattern Recognition 45(1), 521–530. -->

**Equivalence and non-inferiority logic.** The study's deployment questions are not superiority questions. Whether the unified model retains each task's performance (H2b), and whether dynamic balancing improves on tuned static weighting by an amount that matters (H3b), are questions about differences smaller than an operationally meaningful threshold. A classical null hypothesis cannot be confirmed by failure to reject; equivalence logic can, by fixing a margin before the data and asking whether the confidence interval lies entirely inside it — the two one-sided construction behind H3b's 90% interval against $\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}$ and H2b's retention bound $\epsilon$, both frozen in advance so that the tolerance is a design decision rather than a post hoc reading of results. This anchor also encodes the prior the optimization contrast inherits from the literature — that specialized dynamic methods tend to match, not beat, well-tuned simple baselines under equal tuning budgets [@xin2022current; @kurin2022defense; @gama2025uniform] — which is why H3b exists in non-superiority form alongside H3a. <!-- CITE: equivalence-testing methodology, not yet registered. Candidates: Schuirmann (1987), "A comparison of the two one-sided tests procedure and the power approach," J. Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics 15, 657–680; Lakens (2017), "Equivalence Tests," Social Psychological and Personality Science 8(4), 355–362. -->

Together, the five anchors predict the hypothesis families and delimit what each can conclude: sharing predicts both benefit and footprint; conflict theory predicts where interference arises while its rival predicts it may be benign; CMI stratification predicts where transfer varies; distribution shift fixes what any estimate means; and equivalence logic fixes what a difference must exceed to matter.

## Conceptual Framework of the Study

### Software Artifact Conceptual Framework

## Scope and Delimitations

The scope fixes what the study covers; the delimitations are boundaries it draws deliberately, each adopted for a stated reason rather than conceded as a defect.

**Scope.** The corpus is self-annotated and covers $K = 6$ historical benchmark typhoon events (2020–2024), built as a common corpus in which every tweet carries all three label sets; inclusion is by language, not geography — a tweet enters the corpus if and only if it passes the frozen Taglish screen (language identification plus code-mixing index bands), with region serving as a sampling prior for roster selection and never as a filter. The locked event roster and its pre-declared alternates are listed in Chapter 3. The tasks are three: span-level named entity recognition, intent classification, and urgency classification. The encoder is a single shared SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M across all six training arms — three single-task baselines, uniform scalarization, tuned static scalarization, and PCGrad — with task heads trained from scratch under identical architecture parity. @tbl-constants collects the governing constants by name and value ($S = 5$ and $C = 15$–$20$ are adjustable defaults frozen at launch). Hardware is one commodity training and profiling workstation, specified in Chapter 3; no edge device is used, and edge deployment is future work.

: Constants in scope (condensed; the full registry lives in Chapter 3 and the research design). {#tbl-constants}

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| Tasks $T$ | 3 — NER (span-level), Intent, Urgency |
| Folds $K$ | 6 target (minimum 5), one held-out typhoon event per fold |
| Seeds $S$ | 5 per arm per fold |
| Checkpoint windows $C$ | 15–20, on matched fractions of realized optimizer steps |
| Dev split | 15% of training events, stratified by disaster × label |
| Loss normalization | per-example mean reduction, all tasks |
| Retention margin $\epsilon$ | $1.5\times$ pooled single-task seed-SD, frozen before any multitask run |
| Non-superiority margin $\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}$ | 0.01 aggregate Macro-F1 |
| Support threshold | $n \ge 25$ unique examples per stratum × class |
| Deployment protocol | all-resident sequential (primary); load/unload descriptive |
| Workload | all three tasks per request, batch 1 |

**Delimitations.**

1. **Deployed-system estimand.** The study estimates the deployed-system comparison — the unified model trained on all three label sets against single-task baselines trained on their own task's labels over identical inputs — and does not decompose parameter sharing from cross-task supervision, because the deployment question is which configuration to run, not which mechanism acts.
2. **Within-disaster dev leakage.** Model selection uses a dev split drawn from the training events; the leakage this admits is accepted because the policy is identical across arms and therefore protects the comparison, and absolute numbers are read as deployment-realistic.
3. **Evidential partition.** H2a, H2b, H3b, and H4b are carried as descriptive or non-inferiority assessments rather than confirmatory tests, matching each question to the strongest inferential machinery it can support at fold-level resolution.
4. **No cross-hypothesis family-wise control.** Confirmatory tests stand at one-sided $\alpha = .05$ each, with Holm correction applied only within H1b's two-stratum family — a pre-registered declaration, not an oversight.
5. **English-dominant stratum.** Reported descriptively as a contrast; only the Tagalog-dominant and Mixed strata enter the tested family, they being where transfer matters most in the low-resource setting.
6. **Concurrent execution.** Reported only if it completes without memory contention on the profiling machine; all-resident sequential execution is the primary latency baseline.
7. **Fold-level resolution.** Inference operates on $N = K$ fold-level paired observations; the resulting wide intervals are acknowledged rather than corrected, since no estimator recovers statistical resolution that the number of disasters does not contain.
8. **Single platform.** X/Twitter only, over frozen landfall windows for the six historical events selected by pre-registered inclusion criteria, because it is the only platform on which all three corpus requirements hold: a surviving 2020–2024 Philippine typhoon archive; a research-legal convention for releasing annotated collections (tweet identifiers plus annotations only); and a crisis-NLP benchmark literature the results can be compared against. Facebook's research tooling cannot reconstruct retrospective public-post windows and its terms bar resharing; the open alternatives (e.g., Bluesky) postdate most of the roster. Cross-platform generalization (Facebook, Bluesky, and others) is out of scope, deferred to future work.
9. **Tweet mortality.** Handled at release time, not collection time — the corpus is released as tweet identifiers plus annotations only, the platform-standard convention for shareable Twitter datasets.
10. **Taglish by inclusion rule.** Non-Taglish Philippine disaster discourse (Bisaya, Ilocano, Bikol, Waray) is out of scope; the frozen language-identification and CMI screen defines the language boundary, and strata are interpreted within that screen's range-restricted distribution.

## Significance of the Study

The study matters first at the desk where typhoon messages arrive, and then outward through the research communities that can reuse its instruments. Its outputs — the common corpus, the benchmark findings, the inference-efficiency profile, and the gradient-conflict diagnostic — serve the following beneficiaries, each with a concrete use.

**Primary beneficiaries.** *DRRM response coordinators.* The response pillar that Republic Act No. 10121, the Philippine DRRM Act of 2010, assigns to government is operationalized in part through the speed of message triage; a unified model that pre-screens incoming Taglish messages by need and urgency ahead of human review gives coordinators a sorting instrument that runs on commodity hardware. The per-task retention bound (H2b) states plainly what such consolidation costs in task performance, and the recurring under-utilization of DRRM funds documented by the Commission on Audit frames efficiency as an institutional concern rather than an engineering preference [@coa2024drrm]. *Low-resource and code-mixed NLP researchers.* The corpus is the first to pair named entity, intent, and urgency labels on Taglish disaster messages under a common-corpus design, and the benchmark's leave-one-disaster-out protocol with per-task negative-transfer accounting supplies the evaluation setting that in-distribution comparisons in the literature lack.

**Secondary beneficiaries.** *ML engineers deploying unified triage services.* The profiling methodology — batch-1 all-tasks workload, warm-up amortization, all-resident sequential baseline, retention bounds — transfers to any shared-encoder multi-head deployment decision, and the footprint and latency data quantify the trade such consolidation makes. *The regional NLP community.* The study adds supervised fine-tuning evidence on a Southeast Asian encoder family for Taglish, a language the pretraining ecosystem serves thinly; both the confirmation and the failure of transfer expectations here inform encoder choice in the region. *Future researchers.* The pre-registered protocol — freeze ladder, error-control declaration, exact paired inference at fold level, equivalence margins — is a reusable template for benchmark studies with few events, and the released corpus (tweet identifiers plus annotations) is a foundation for replication and extension.

**Tertiary beneficiaries.** *Affected communities and public-information officers.* If pre-screening holds up under the study's measured bounds, distress messages reach the appropriate desk sooner, and information officers work over categorized streams rather than raw feeds. The study contributes a sorting instrument and its limits, not an automated decision-maker; human judgment remains in the loop by design.

## Definitions of Terms
